metaDesc: An unhurried temple-hopping day in Sing Buri, Thailand: start with one of the country's largest reclining Buddhas at Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi, then the giant standing Buddha at Wat Phikun Thong, and the Buddha-casting workshop at Wat Sawang Arom — with timings, the route, and Mae La snakehead fish along the way.

h1:
Sing Buri Temple Day Trip
3 Temples in One Day
intro: Sing Buri is a small province you can drive around and visit temples comfortably in a single day. The three temples people usually pair together are Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi with its giant reclining Buddha, Wat Phikun Thong with its huge blessing-pose Buddha, and Wat Sawang Arom, which is still a working Buddha-image workshop. We've laid out the route so you never have to double back, with a midday stop for Mae La snakehead fish — the dish this province is known for.
chips: 🐟 Stop for Mae La snakehead fish

blocks.html: If you only have a single day and want to visit Sing Buri's temples without rushing, these three are the most balanced set. They sit in and around the Mueang district, not far apart — under half an hour of driving between each stop. Start a little early so the sun isn't harsh and the crowds are still thin. The nice thing is that all three feel different: one stands out for its old reclining Buddha, one for its towering standing Buddha, and one for its craftsmanship — so you never get bored seeing the same thing twice.

The easiest way to get around is your own car or a rental, since the temples are spread out in different directions and local public transport is limited. Coming from Bangkok, drive up the Asia Highway (Route 32) and you'll reach Sing Buri town in about an hour and a half.

blocks.label: Morning
blocks.title: Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi — the giant reclining Buddha

items.activity: Leave your accommodation in Sing Buri town and head for Chakkrasi sub-district
items.note: About 4 km from town — under a 15-minute drive

items.activity: Enter Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi Worawihan and pay respects to the reclining Buddha
items.note: The reclining Buddha is over 47 m long, an old stucco image and one of the largest in Thailand

items.activity: Walk through the ordination hall and see Phra Kan and Phra Kaeo inside the temple
items.note: This is a royal temple — shady and relaxed, with plenty of room to take photos

items.activity: Set off toward Wat Phikun Thong
items.note: Drive south along the Noi River for about 16 km — roughly 25 minutes

blocks.label: Late morning–noon
blocks.title: Wat Phikun Thong + a Mae La snakehead fish lunch

items.activity: Arrive at Wat Phikun Thong, a royal temple, and pay respects to the Great Buddha (Luang Pho Yai)
items.note: Phra Phuttha Suwan Mongkhon Maha Muni (Luang Pho Yai) is a huge blessing-pose Buddha covered in gold mosaic

items.activity: Visit the Luang Pho Phae museum to see his monastic belongings and history
items.note: Luang Pho Phae was a famous monk of Sing Buri, deeply revered by locals

items.activity: Break for lunch — Mae La snakehead fish
items.note: The Mae La–Bang Rachan area has several grilled-snakehead spots; pick a roadside place that's busy

items.activity: Head back toward town for Wat Sawang Arom
items.note: It's in Ton Pho sub-district near the Chao Phraya River — about a 25–30 minute drive

blocks.label: Afternoon
blocks.title: Wat Sawang Arom — a working Buddha-casting workshop

items.activity: Arrive at Wat Sawang Arom in Ton Pho sub-district
Watch the artisans cast Buddha images, a craft passed down from the Thonburi casting lineage
items.note: This temple still makes Buddha images for real, so you can watch the work up close

items.activity: Visit the nang yai (giant shadow-puppet) museum with over 300 antique puppets
items.note: It's one of Thailand's most complete collections of nang yai puppets

items.activity: Photograph the ordination hall and the replica Buddha footprint, then wrap up the trip
items.note: Before heading home, grab some sun-dried snakehead fish or local Sing Buri souvenirs

blocks.text: Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi — starting with the giant reclining Buddha

blocks.html: Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi Worawihan, in Chakkrasi sub-district of Mueang district, is a royal temple. The highlight is its huge stucco reclining Buddha, over 47 m long — an old image considered one of the largest in the country. The Buddha sits in a long hall you can walk all the way around, and standing beside it makes you feel tiny. It's a great way to start the day because the hall is airy and the crowds are still light.

items: Main place to pay respects — the reclining Buddha in the long hall; people pray here for health and peace of mind
Phra Kan and Phra Kaeo — old Buddha images in the temple you can stop and pay respects to in the same area
Atmosphere — a wide temple courtyard with shady trees, easy to walk and photograph without rushing

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: Come before 10 a.m. for nice light and gentle sun. The reclining Buddha hall is fairly open, so you can photograph the whole image without crowds in the way.

blocks.text: Wat Phikun Thong — the Great Buddha in blessing pose

blocks.html: Wat Phikun Thong, a royal temple, sits on the bank of the Noi River about 16 km from town. Locals often call it "Wat Luang Pho Phae" because the famous monk Luang Pho Phae once stayed here. The spot that draws the most people is the Great Buddha — Phra Phuttha Suwan Mongkhon Maha Muni, a colossal blessing-pose Buddha covered entirely in gold mosaic and visible from a distance. The grounds also include the Luang Pho Phae museum, where you can walk through his history and monastic belongings.

items.name: The Great Buddha
items.blurb: A huge blessing-pose Buddha covered in gold mosaic — you can walk up to pay respects right at the base

items.name: Luang Pho Phae museum
items.blurb: Displays of Luang Pho Phae's history and belongings — good for anyone interested in Sing Buri's revered monks

items.name: Cosmos flower field
items.blurb: In the cool season around January, the temple opens a cosmos field for photos (only at certain times)

blocks.title: Check before a cool-season visit
blocks.html: The cosmos field isn't there year-round — it mostly blooms around January. If you're coming specifically to photograph the flowers, check the temple's page before you set off to be sure.

blocks.text: Wat Sawang Arom — a temple that still casts Buddha images

blocks.html: Wrap up the trip at Wat Sawang Arom in Ton Pho sub-district, within the town area. What makes this temple special is that it's still a working Buddha-image workshop, carrying on a craft inherited from the Thonburi casting lineage. Walk in and you'll see artisans shaping and finishing actual Buddha images — not just looking at finished pieces. The temple also keeps more than 300 antique nang yai (giant shadow puppets) and has a nang yai museum to visit, making it a place where you can pay respects and watch fine craftsmanship in one stop.

items: The casting yard — watch artisans actually at work, a sight you rarely see at ordinary temples
Nang yai museum — over 300 antique giant shadow puppets, still playable in performances
Ordination hall and replica Buddha footprint — decades-old work worth a slow look at the details

blocks.text: What to eat along the way

blocks.html: Since you're in Sing Buri, don't miss Mae La snakehead fish — the firm-fleshed freshwater fish this province is famous for. On the drive back from Wat Phikun Thong into town, you'll pass the Mae La–Bang Rachan area lined with grilled-snakehead shops. In town there are plenty of boat-noodle spots too. Have a filling lunch before the afternoon temple so you can enjoy it on a happy stomach.

items.name: Grilled Mae La snakehead fish (Mae La–Bang Rachan area)
items.blurb: Fresh snakehead grilled in salt, firm-fleshed, eaten with seafood dipping sauce and neem shoots with sweet fish sauce. It's the dish people come to Sing Buri specifically to eat. There are several roadside shops — pick the busy one.
items.meta: Lunch · a whole grilled fish from about ฿250 depending on size

items.name: Sing Buri boat noodles
items.blurb: Rich nam tok boat noodles, Sing Buri style. Small bowls, so order several. A light bite to keep you going before the next stop.

items.name: Sun-dried snakehead fish (souvenir)
items.blurb: Made from Mae La snakehead — fry it up with rice porridge or buy it to take home. You'll find it at roadside shops and town markets.

blocks.text: Tips to keep the day running smoothly

items: Use your own car or a rental — the temples are in different directions and public transport is limited, so driving is by far the easiest
Start early — leaving around 8:30 a.m. lets you hit all three temples, have lunch, and get back before evening with time to spare
Dress modestly — these are royal temples, so a top with sleeves and knee-length trousers or skirt keeps things respectful
Bring cash — offering flowers, incense and candles, plus small souvenir shops, are mostly cash only

faq.q: Can you visit all 3 of these Sing Buri temples in one day?
faq.a: Easily. Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi, Wat Phikun Thong, and Wat Sawang Arom are in and around Mueang district, with under half an hour of driving between each. Start around 8:30 a.m., visit all three, have a Mae La snakehead fish lunch, and you'll be back before evening.

faq.q: Which temple should I start with?
faq.a: Start with Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi in the morning, since it's close to town and the hall is airy with few people. Follow with Wat Phikun Thong in the late morning, then lunch around Mae La, and finish at Wat Sawang Arom in the afternoon. This route means you never double back.

faq.q: How do you get to Sing Buri from Bangkok?
faq.a: Drive up the Asia Highway (Route 32); it takes about an hour and a half to reach Sing Buri town. Once there, use your own car or a rental, since the temples are spread out in different directions and public transport is limited.

faq.q: What are Wat Sawang Arom's opening hours?
faq.a: According to published information, the temple is open Mon–Fri around 09:00–16:00 and Sat–Sun 08:30–17:00. If you want to watch the artisans casting Buddha images and see the nang yai museum, come during opening hours.

faq.q: What's good to eat around there?
faq.a: The local specialty is grilled Mae La snakehead fish, with shops lined up around Mae La–Bang Rachan; the fish is firm and eaten with seafood dipping sauce. In town, try Sing Buri boat noodles, and pick up some sun-dried snakehead fish as a souvenir to take home.
